prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms made timekeeping at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B009, Katori and Ye, as a single prize part. Round 1 showed that all eight of us land on the same pair, and the chair rightly warns that part of this is movement after the opening ballots. So I tested my own position against the chair's questions instead of leaning on the count. On discovery versus instrument: the criterion rewards a discovery or an invention, and the magic wavelength is an invention with a physical idea behind it. It is a statement about how to engineer the atom's coupling to light so that the trap does not shift the transition, and it turns a many-atom ensemble from a liability into a resource. In statistical terms the gain is quantum projection noise falling with atom number, which is what made 1e-18 stability reachable. That is a different idea from the comb (a ruler for optical frequencies) and from ion control (single quantum systems). On delivered results: the clocks are already used as instruments for physics. Intercomparisons between laboratories and species constrain variation of fundamental constants, and resolving the gravitational redshift over sub-millimetre height differences within a single atomic sample is a relativistic test that earlier clocks could not perform. I rely on recalled values for these numbers, but the qualitative point does not depend on them. Dark-matter searches and relativistic geodesy are still partly prospective, and I say so. On the wording of the citation: I would name the invention (optical lattice clocks, magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms) and the performance level (10^-18), and I would not name a record figure as the achievement, because that number will be superseded. The concept and first demonstration belong to Katori, and the move to the accuracy and many-body frontier belongs to Ye's group. On timing: I would not wait for the redefinition of the second. The redefinition is a decision by metrology bodies. The invention has been reproduced and is already infrastructure regardless of when that decision is taken.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that this is the third precision atomic-physics prize in about twenty years (2005, 2012, and now), and some members will see a metrology instrument and not a new phenomenon. Eriksson put this sharply: if the committee prefers a change in what physicists can think about over what they can measure, B009 loses to topological insulators or lattice quantum simulation, and I cannot dismiss that argument. Credit is the second problem. Two names leave out Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat, the PTB and NIST groups and the Yb and Hg communities, and the 1e-18 milestones were reached in several laboratories. A citation can state what it credits, but it cannot make the omission disappear. Third, the payoff in fundamental physics is still mostly in the form of constraints and projections and not a positive discovery, as Danielsson noted. I judge these to be real qualifications, but not a reason to move away from the cleanest and most thoroughly reproduced candidate on the list.

responses.point: Kroll supports B009 and states in his round-1 file that the comb and ion-clock lineage should be handled by the citation, and also discloses a research period in Hall's laboratory, where Ye trained, asking the committee to consider whether recusal is needed.
responses.response: I agree that the lineage question belongs in the citation. I would go further and say that the citation should name the invention (magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms) and so exclude the clockwork of the comb and the single-ion route by construction. On the disclosure, I think recording it is sufficient. Kroll did not work with Ye and has no stake in the result, and a shared laboratory lineage in a field this small is hard to avoid. I would ask the chair to note the disclosure in the minutes and to have Kroll's vote counted. What I would watch instead is the effect on his judgment of the lineage: it argues for reading Kroll's enthusiasm with the same care that Johansson and Olsson ask for their own. His round-1 file does this honestly, since it states the case against as clearly as the case for.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from IceCube first and clocks fifth to B009, but warns that eight-of-eight ranking should not be mistaken for depth of scientific weight, and notes that the clocks have not yet produced a fundamental-physics result of their own.
responses.response: The caution is fair and I have tried to apply it to myself. The breadth of support is not an argument, and I would not cite it in a public position. What I can offer instead is the scientific content: the magic-wavelength condition, the statistical gain from interrogating many atoms, and independent reproduction in Sr and Yb. On the claim that there is no fundamental-physics result, I would separate two things. The clocks have not found new physics, which is also true of most precision tests in the history of the field. They have produced new measured constraints and a new kind of relativistic test, and the redshift across sub-millimetre height differences is the clearest example. A prize does not need a positive discovery of new physics to recognise an invention that has changed what is measurable. I also hold the point that you made against Kroll, that the citation must differ visibly from 2005 and 2012, and I have written mine around the invention and not around clocks in general.

responses.point: Pearce moved his own first choice, IceCube (B052), to an alternative, says the credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering and the precursors is harder to settle, and no longer insists on it this year. He also said he does not put B010 among his alternatives because of its split credit.
responses.response: I accept the second point and it affects me: B010 is a weaker alternative than I made it in round 1. Zoller's credit overlaps with B014, and four credited names do not fit a three-person limit without an explicit choice that nobody has made. I keep it as a second alternative because of the scientific content, but I do not claim that it is ready. On B052, I agree with you that the diffuse flux is established and the discovery is real, and I think this is a candidate the committee should take up in a coming year with a settled credit. The flux has several hundred collaborators and AMANDA and Baikal precursors, and when the member who knows the field best would credit two names and not three, I cannot argue for the supplied trio. That is why I leave B052 out of my alternatives rather than list it with names I would want changed.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B009, argues that the trustworthiness of the performance claims rests on understood relativistic atomic structure, blackbody and polarisability physics, and says the committee should resolve B014 versus B010 as one question because Zoller sits in both.
responses.response: Her first point is the strongest answer to the instrument objection. A systematic uncertainty at 1e-18 is a claim that the atomic theory is under control to that level, and that is physics in the ordinary sense. On Zoller, I agree and I have dropped B014 from my alternatives for the reason she gives: if the committee ever prefers a quantum-information or lattice-simulation prize, it should decide the Cirac-Zoller and Bloch-Greiner-Esslinger-Zoller question together, and not leave Zoller to be placed by a vote on two different ballot IDs. I do not think that decision is needed this year, because B009 does not depend on it. Her disciplinary-bias disclosure is fair and I extend the same to myself: I am a theorist of complex systems and not an atomic physicist, so I rely on the committee's atomic physicists for the experimental history, and on this point I note that Lindroth and Kroll agree on the order of the proposal and the demonstrations.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B041 first to B009 and states that B009 would drop for him if the committee prefers a change in what physicists can think about over what they can measure, and notes that B018 and B010 opened new fields.
responses.response: This is the most serious challenge to my position, and I think it deserves a direct answer and not a vote. I do not think the criterion is limited to new questions. Optical lattice clocks did change what is possible to ask: comparing clocks across a height difference of a millimetre or across a continent turns time into a probe of gravity and of constants. But if the committee reads the criterion as Eriksson does, then the strongest rival is B018, which I list first among my alternatives. Its scientific weight is clear. The obstacle is the one Danielsson and Lindroth raised, that the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal and the three-dimensional work lie outside the three supplied names, and with a three-person limit this cannot be repaired by adding a name. A prize that I would have to defend as incomplete is worse than a prize on a narrower but cleaner claim. If the committee resolved the omissions I would reopen the comparison, but on the evidence in front of us I do not move.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a discovery-class invention or as instrumentation following the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I have argued the first but this is a judgment and not a fact.
Whether a two-name citation can carry the narrower claim (magic-wavelength lattice, concept and realization) without understating Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lisdat and the PTB, NIST, Yb and Hg groups.

I rely on recalled figures for accuracy, for the redshift measurement over sub-millimetre height differences, and for the status of the redefinition of the second, and I have not verified them independently.
How Zoller's credit should be handled if the committee comes back to B010 or B014 in a later year.
If the committee wanted a two-part prize, I still have no second part that fits within the three-person limit and has settled credit.
statement.conflict_note: No change: I disclose no specific conflict. My profile documents no connection to Katori, Ye, or any other credited candidate, and my supervisors and co-authors do not overlap with them. I am a theorist of complex systems and not an atomic physicist, so I rely on colleagues for the experimental history of lattice clocks. I note, as a matter of procedure, the disclosures by Kroll (Hall laboratory), Johansson (circuit QED), Olsson (electron microscopy) and Lindroth (atomic-physics proximity), and I consider that recording them is sufficient for B009.
